idiom_name: std::convert::identity as the do-nothing base case; |x| x where a closure fits
implementation_notes: Rust ships the canonical identity as a standard-library function: std::convert::identity is pub const fn identity<T>(x: T) -> T (stable 1.33.0, re-exported from core::convert per RFC 2306) and is #[inline] + monomorphized, so it is a zero-cost fn item usable wherever an impl Fn(T) -> T is expected - as the no-op branch of a strategy if/else, as the base case of Iterator::fold, or as filter_map(identity) to keep the Some variants of an iterator of Option<T>. The closure |x| x is the local fallback where a fn item does not fit, with one documented divergence: a closure may coerce its argument (deref/unsized/lifetime), while identity never changes the type. There is no compose operator, so the neutral element of composition is spelled as a fold over impl Fn steps seeded with identity; the comparator analogue of the binary identity (a, b) -> 0 is the natural-order default - sort_by_key with an identity key (F: FnMut(&T) -> K, K: Ord), or plain sort() where T: Ord - and Ordering::Equal is the neutral element of the (T, T) -> Ordering comparator monoid. The classic hand-written strategy/visitor structure is justified only when the transformation set is discovered at runtime; identity then occupies the empty Box<dyn Fn> slot.
pitfalls: identity moves its input: for a non-Copy T, identity(x) consumes x and the original binding is dead afterwards - value flow GC languages ignore is real here; pass identity(&x) or a reference form when the value is still needed.

|x| x is not always equivalent to identity: a closure may coerce its argument (deref, unsized, lifetime coercion), while std::convert::identity never changes the type - swapping one for the other can silently change the parameter type at a coercion site.

std::convert::identity is defined only for Sized types (fn identity<T: Sized>); a position handing out unsized values (&dyn Trait, [u8]) cannot take it - fall back to a generic bound or an explicit coercion.

filter_map(identity) flattens Option<T> and drops the Nones, map(identity) does not flatten, and .flatten() is usually clearer - an identity meant as 'do nothing' can silently change the iterator's element type.

A unary identity does not satisfy a comparator: slice::sort_by expects FnMut(&T, &T) -> Ordering; the neutral choice is the derived natural order (sort_by_key with an identity key, or sort() where T: Ord). The wrong-arity mistake is a compile error, not a silent runtime bug.

Mixing identity with closures in one collection forces unification at fn-pointer type (fn items are distinct zero-sized types) or Box<dyn Fn(T) -> T>; the boxed form erases monomorphization and reintroduces a small dynamic-call cost that the bare fn item never has.
